--- pagetitle: "Linear Regression: Review" editor: source format: revealjs: html-math-method: mathjax chalkboard: true incremental: true theme: [default, custom.scss] height: 900 width: 1600 slide-number: c auto-stretch: false callout-appearance: simple pdf-max-pages-per-slide: 2 menu: side: right numbers: true execute: echo: true warning: false message: false --- ::: {.center}


[Linear Regression: Review]{.custom-title}

[Michael Pearce]{.custom-subtitle} [Math 243]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Outline ::: {.nonincremental} In today's class, we will... - Review simple and multiple linear regression - Perform inference for linear regression models - Implement linear regression in `R` ::: # Foundations ## Linear Regression Suppose we have: ::: {.nonincremental} - one or more **predictors**, $(X_1, X_2, \dots , X_p)$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - a **quantitative response variable** $Y$, where $$ Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_p) + \epsilon $$ where $\epsilon$ ("epsilon") is random "error" or "noise" ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} The **simplest form** for $f$ is a **linear function**: $$ f(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p $$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} If $Y$ depends on.. - 1 predictor, $X$, we have **Simple Linear Regression** (SLR) - $\geq2$ predictors, $X_1,\dots,X_p$, we have **Multiple Linear Regression** (MLR) ::: ## Approximations and Estimates **The relationship $f$ between $Y$ and $X_1, \dots, X_p$ is rarely linear!** ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - linear models are still good approximations, often ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Problem:** Even if $f$ is linear, we still do not know its parameters ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Solution:** Using data, we estimate the parameters and the model: $$ \hat{f} (x_1, \dots, x_p) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_1 + \dots + \hat{\beta}_px_p $$ - $\hat{\beta_k}$ are *estimates* of the "true" $\beta_k$ - Obtain $\hat{\beta_k}$ via **least-squares**: Values of $\hat{\beta_k}$ that minimize the total squared distance between data and the regression line, $$\sum_{i=1}^n \Big(y_i - \hat{f}(x_{1i},\dots,x_{pi})\Big)^2$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} If $f$ is NOT linear, then: - we're estimating an *approximation* of the relationship between $Y$ and $X_1, \dots, X_p$ ::: ## Categorical Predictors It's most common to have quantitative predictor variables, but categorical (i.e. qualitative) predictors are also common. ::: {.nonincremental} + Example: Penguin species (Adelie, Gentoo, Chinstrap) + Example: State of residence (Oregon, Washington, etc.) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Unfortunately, we can't directly add categorical variables to regression equations, since **can't perform algebra** with them! For example, consider the following regression model: $$\hat{\text{Income}} = 30{,}000 + 5{,}000\times\text{Oregon}$$ What is $5{,}000\times\text{Oregon}$?! ::: ## Categorical Predictors: Indicator Variables To perform algebra with categories, we usually convert each **level** of a categorical variable into an **indicator variable** (denoted with letter $I$): $$I\{\text{Oregon}\} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X = \text{Oregon} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Returning to our example on the previous slide, we now have $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\text{Income}} &= 30 + 5I\{\text{Oregon}\} \\ &=\begin{cases} 30+5(1) & \text{if } X=\text{Oregon}\\ 30+ 5(0) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned}$$ ::: ## Categorical Predictors: Number of Indicator Variables When converting a single categorical predictor into indicator variable(s), there is always **1 fewer indicator variable than there are levels**. ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Example:** Suppose $X=\text{Heads or Tails}$ (2 levels $\implies$ 1 indicator variable): $$I\{Heads\} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X=\text{Heads}\\ 0 & \text{if } X=\text{Tails} \end{cases}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Example:** Suppose $X=\text{Blue, Green, or Yellow}$ (3 levels $\implies$ 2 indicator variables): $$I\{Blue\} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X=\text{Blue}\\ 0 & \text{if } X=\text{Green or Yellow} \end{cases}$$ $$I\{Green\} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X=\text{Green}\\ 0 & \text{if } X=\text{Blue or Yellow} \end{cases}$$ $\implies$ if $I\{Blue\}=I\{Green\}=0$, then $X$ must be Yellow! ::: ## Example Suppose we model Income ($Y$) vs Age ($X_1$) and State $X_2\in\{OR, WA, CA\}$ ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} $$\hat{\text{Income}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{Age} + \beta_2 I\{\text{OR}\} + \beta_3 I\{\text{WA}\}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$\begin{cases} \beta_0+\beta_1\text{Age} & \text{if State=CA}\\ (\beta_0+\beta_2)+\beta_1\text{Age} & \text{if State=OR}\\ (\beta_0+\beta_3)+\beta_1\text{Age} & \text{if State=WA} \end{cases}$$ ::: # Interpretation ## Coefficient Interpretation Suppose we estimate a linear regression model, $\hat{f}$: $$ \hat{f} (x_1, \dots, x_p) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_1 + \dots + \hat{\beta}_px_p $$ How do we interpret the coefficients? ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Interpretation of coefficients is an **essential** statistical skill - Don't be creative here! **Careful and precise** interpretation is necessary. - Always include **context**: Relate interpretations to the actual data/variables studied. ::: ## Coefficient Interpretation (SLR) We start with simple linear regression: $$ \hat{f} (x_1) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1} x_1 $$ ::: {.nonincremental} - **Intercept, $\hat{\beta_0}$**: When $x_1=0$, we expect $Y$ to be $\hat{\beta_0}$, on average. $$\begin{aligned} \text{Why? }\quad \hat{f} (x_1=0) &= \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1}(0)\\ &=\hat\beta_0 \end{aligned}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Slope, $\hat{\beta_1}$**: For every one-unit increase in $x_1$, we expect $Y$ to change by $\hat{\beta_1}$, on average. $$\begin{aligned} \text{Why? }\quad \hat{f} (x_1+1) -\hat{f} (x_1) &= \Big(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1}(x_1+1)\Big) - \Big(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1}(x_1)\Big)\\ &=\hat\beta_1 \end{aligned}$$ ::: ## Coefficient Interpretation (MLR) What about MLR? $$ \hat{f} (x_1,\dots,x_p) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1} x_1 + \dots + \hat{\beta_p} x_p $$ ::: {.nonincremental} - **Intercept, $\hat{\beta_0}$**: When $x_1=x_2=\dots=x_p=0$, we expect $Y$ to be $\hat{\beta_0}$, on average. $$\begin{aligned} \text{Why? }\quad \hat{f} (x_1=x_2=\dots=x_p=0) &= \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1}(0)+\dots+\hat{\beta_p}(0)\\ &=\hat\beta_0 \end{aligned}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Slope, $\hat{\beta_j}$**: For every one-unit increase in $x_j$, we expect $Y$ to change by $\hat{\beta_j}$, on average, holding all else constant. $$\begin{aligned} \text{Why? }\quad \hat{f} (x_1+1) -\hat{f} (x_1) &= \Big(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1}(x_1+1)\Big) - \Big(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta_1}(x_1)\Big)\\ &=\hat\beta_1 \end{aligned}$$ ::: ## Word of Caution: Categorical Variables Suppose we have the model $$ \hat{Income} = \beta_0 + \beta_1Age + \beta_2 I\{State=\text{Oregon}\} $$ where $Age$ is a quantitative variable and $State\in\{\text{Oregon,Washington}\}$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Interpretations: + $\beta_0$: Expected $Income$ when $Age=0$ and State=Washington (the **baseline level**) on average. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} + $\beta_1$: Precisely as usual! ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} + $\beta_2$: Comparing someone from Oregon to someone from Washington (the baseline), we expect Income to change by $\beta_2$ on average, holding Age constant. ::: ## Other Advice ::: {.nonincremental} Always, always, always... 1. Include the phrases "on average" and "expected" in your interpretations. If they aren't there, it's **wrong!** 2. If there are **multiple variables** in your model, include the phrase "holding all else constant" (or something very similar contextual) 3. Include **context**, not mathematical symbols ::: # Statistical Inference in Regression ## Conditions for Using Linear Regression **In *traditional* regression analyses, we must satisfy certain conditions:** ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 1. **Linearity:** The relationship between predictor and response variables must be approximately linear - Check using scatterplot/residual plot ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2. **Independence:** The observations should be independent of one another. - Often "contextual"; sometimes can be seen in scatterplot/residual plot ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 3. **Normality:** The distribution of residuals should be normally distributed, and centered at 0 **at every "slice" of the predictor variable** - Histogram of residuals - Q-Q plot of residuals ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 4. **Equal Variability:** Variance of residuals should be roughly constant across data set. - Check using residual plot. ::: ::: {.fragment} Abbreviated using acronym **LINE** ::: ## 1) Linearity **Linearity:** The relationship between $X$ and $Y$ must be approximately linear ::: {.nonincremental} - Points should be evenly distributed above and below the regression line **at each "slice" of X** ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Mathematically:** $Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon$ where $E(\epsilon \ | \ X) = 0$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: If data is non-linear... - Slope does not adequately describe relationship - Predictions can be very inaccurate ::: ## 1) Linearity Looking at residual plots is also very useful when checking this! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## 2) Independent Observations **Independence:** The observations should be independent of one another (given $X$) ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Mathematically:** $\epsilon_i$ and $\epsilon_j$ are independent (given $X$) ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} If observations are not independent... - Slope and intercept estimates may be more variable in sample - Inference about the population may be misleading ::: ## 3) Normality (of Residuals) **Normality of Residuals:** The distribution of residuals should be normally distributed and centered at 0 **at every "slice" of $X$** ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Mathematically:** $\epsilon \ | \ X \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$ ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} If residuals are non-Normal... - Some predictions can be very inaccurate - Inference about the population may be misleading ::: ## 4) Equal Variability (of Residuals) **Equal Variability:** Variance of residuals should be roughly constant across data set. ::: {.nonincremental} - **Mathematically:** $var(\epsilon \ | \ X) = \sigma^2$ for constant $\sigma^2$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} If residuals don't have equal variability... - Inference about the population may be misleading - (Potential) outliers in high-variability range are more influential ::: ::: {.notes} Residual plots are also useful for checking this! ::: ## 4) Equal Variability (of Residuals) **Equal Variability:** Variance of residuals should be roughly constant across data set. ::: {.nonincremental} - **Mathematically:** $var(\epsilon \ | \ X) = \sigma^2$ for constant $\sigma^2$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: If residuals don't have equal variability... - Inference about the population may be misleading - (Potential) outliers in high-variability range are more influential Residual plots are also useful for checking this! ::: ## Statistical Inference With a fitted linear model, we want to make **inferences**. ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Our Question:** Learn about a **parameter** that summarizes a **population** - e.g., $\beta_0$ is "true" average $Y$ when $X_1=\dots=X_p=0$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Solution:** Estimate a **statistic** from our **sample** - e.g., fitted $\hat{\beta_0}$ is a good guess for $\beta_0$ - We don't know "how good" an estimate $\hat{\beta_0}$ is! ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Tools:** - Confidence intervals - Hypothesis tests ::: ::: {.fragment} Both require us learn the statistic's **sampling distribution** ::: ## Sampling Distribution **Sampling Distribution:** the distribution of our statistic *across different random samples* (hypothetically) ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Ex:** Estimating the Mean GPA of Reed students - **Parameter:** Mean GPA of All Reed students - **Statistic:** Mean GPA of a sample of 50 Reed students ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="49%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="49%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index="3"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="3"} **Standard Error:** the standard deviation of the sample distribution ::: ## Confidence Intervals **Confidence Intervals** give estimates **and** express our uncertainty in those estimates. ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} A $C$-level (e.g., 0.95-level or 95%) confidence interval for a **parameter $\beta_j$** using the **statistic $\hat{\beta_j}$** means... - In $C$% of random samples, the true $\beta_j$ will be contained in the interval. - **NOT** a C% "chance" that $\beta_j$ is in the interval. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Typically create intervals in two ways: 1) Bootstrap method **← will review this in a later lecture** ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2) Theory-based inference - Find sampling distribution using statistical theory (like Central Limit Theorem) - Middle $C$% constitutes a proper confidence interval ::: ## Hypothesis Tests (Steps 1-3 of 5) A formal statistical process of testing hypotheses about a **parameter ($\beta_j$)** ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 1. **Present research question and identify Hypotheses** - Null Hypothesis ($H_0$): $\beta_j = \gamma$ for some $\gamma$ - Alternative Hypothesis ($H_A$): $\beta_j > \gamma$ or $\beta_j < \gamma$ or $\beta_j \neq \gamma$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 2. **Choose a Test Statistic ($T$)** - Usually a function of our statistic ($\hat{\beta_j}$) - e.g., turning our statistic into something that *looks like* a z-score: $$ T = \frac{\hat{\beta_j} - \gamma}{\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta_j})} $$ - We observe $T = t$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 3. **Determine the null (sampling) distribution of $T$** - Theory-based inference tools, here! ::: ## Hypothesis Tests (Steps 4-5) ::: {.nonincremental} 1. Present research question and identify **Hypotheses ($H_0$ and $H_A$)** 2. Choose a **Test Statistic ($T$)** 3. Determine the **null (sampling) distribution** of $T$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 4. **Calculate the p-Value**: ::: {.center} p-Value: probability of what happened in reality (or something more extreme), assuming that the null is true. ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} 5. **Use the P-Value to make a conclusion on the research question** - **Traditional:** "Reject" $H_0$ if $p<\alpha$, a **significance level**; "fail to reject $H_0$" otherwise. - **Modern (Better!):** $p$ provides **"strength of evidence"** against $H_0$. - e.g., $p=0.001$ provides strong evidence that $H_0$ isn't true! ::: ## Statistical Inference in Regression **Parameters:** ::: {.nonincremental} - Assume there is a linear relationship between $Y$ and $X$: \begin{align*} Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon \end{align*} ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **$\beta_0$, $\beta_1$ are the parameters!** **Q:** In words, what does it mean if $\beta_1 = 0$? How about it $\beta_1 \neq 0$? ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Statistics:** **$\hat{\beta}_0$, $\hat{\beta}_1$** estimated from our sample data! - For theory-based inference, model must satisfy all LINE conditions - Use `R` to perform confidence intervals or conduct hypothesis tests. ::: ## `R` code Consider the following regression between High School Graduate Rate ($Y$) and Poverty Rates ($X$): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod <- lm(Graduates ~ Poverty, data = poverty) get_regression_table(mod) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 7 term estimate std_error statistic p_value lower_ci upper_ci 1 intercept 96.2 1.34 71.6 0 93.5 98.9 2 Poverty -0.898 0.114 -7.86 0 -1.13 -0.668 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Hypothesis Test for $\beta_1$** - `std_error` (0.114) and `statistic` (-7.86) - `p_value` --- corresponding p-value ($\approx 0$) for the *two-sided test*, $$H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \qquad H_a: \beta_1 \neq 0$$ ::: ## `R` code Consider the following regression between High School Graduate Rate ($Y$) and Poverty Rates ($X$): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod <- lm(Graduates ~ Poverty, data = poverty) get_regression_table(mod) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 7 term estimate std_error statistic p_value lower_ci upper_ci 1 intercept 96.2 1.34 71.6 0 93.5 98.9 2 Poverty -0.898 0.114 -7.86 0 -1.13 -0.668 ``` ::: ::: **95% Confidence Interval** - 95% CI for $\beta_1$ is (`lower_ci`,`upper_ci`)=(-1.13,-0.668) # Case Study ## Credit Card Debt The `Credit` dataset in the `ISLR` package contains (fabricated) credit card debt and other financial and demographic information for 400 individuals. ::: {.fragment} **Goal:** Build a model that predicts credit debt given financial and demographic information ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Consider Debt (`Balance`) as a function of Credit Limit (`Limit`) and Income in \$1000 (`Income`) ::: ::: {.fragment} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%" .smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: $$R = 0.86 \qquad \widehat{Debt} = -292.8 + 0.17 \cdot \textrm{Limit}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="45%" .smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: $$R = 0.46 \qquad \widehat{Debt} = 246.51 + 6.048 \cdot \textrm{Income}$$ ::: :::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Both predictors have some explanatory power for Debt -- and **positive correlations** ::: ## Multiple Regression for Debt Let's find the MLR model: ::: {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mod<-lm(Balance ~ Limit + Income, data = Credit) get_regression_table(mod) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 7 term estimate std_error statistic p_value lower_ci upper_ci 1 intercept -385. 19.5 -19.8 0 -423. -347. 2 Limit 0.264 0.006 45.0 0 0.253 0.276 3 Income -7.66 0.385 -19.9 0 -8.42 -6.91 ``` ::: ::: ::: $$\widehat{Debt} = -385.179 + 0.264 \cdot \textrm{Limit} - 7.663 \cdot \textrm{Income}$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - For an individual with a $\$0$ credit limit and no income, we expect $-\$385$ in Debt, on average. (*nonsensical*) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - As Credit Limit increases by $\$1$, Debt is expected to **increase** by $\$0.26$, on average, *holding Income fixed* ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - As Income increases by $\$1000$, Debt is expected to **decrease** by $\$7.66$, on average, *holding Credit Limit fixed* Wait...**the coefficient on Income switched direction!! How?** ::: ## Income and Credit Limit First let's consider the relationship between Income and Credit Limit ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Remember that Credit Limit was more correlated with Debt than Income was ($R = 0.86$ vs. $R = 0.46$). ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_Regression_Review_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=45%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} **As income increases, credit limit tends to increase as well!** ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - In the SLR model between Debt and Income, increases in Income also implies increases in Credit Limit ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - But in the MLR model, **we *fix* Credit Limit, and *then* increase Income independently** ::: ## "Fixing" Credit Limit Let's consider what the model is saying after we "fix" credit limit $$\widehat{Debt} = -385.179 + 0.264 \cdot \textrm{Limit} \textcolor{red}{- 7.663} \cdot \textrm{Income}$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Consider two people **who have equal Credit Limits** - One person has a higher income than the other person ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **MLR model:** the person with the higher Income tends to have less Debt - **Q:** Why does this make sense? ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Higher income means they have more resources to pay off their debt! - Maybe the reason they have higher income is because they tend to spend less! - Higher income may be associated with other factors (e.g., higher education) ::: ## Assumptions, Revisited In Multiple Linear Regression, we still must check the LINE Conditions: $$\text{Linearity, Independence, Normality, Equal Variance}$$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} There are two minor differences: - For independence, we (often) want to avoid models with **"multicollinearity"**: some predictors are severely correlated with one another. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - When checking assumptions using residual plots, we must show residuals vs. *predicted values* (instead of $X$). ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} When LINE conditions are met, we can conduct inference just like before!! - Same `R` code! ::: ## Hypothesis Test for *all* $\hat{\beta}_k$? We know how to do hypothesis tests for each *individual* $\beta_k$... $$ H_0: \beta_k = 0 \quad \quad vs. \quad \quad H_A: \beta_k \neq 0 $$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Can we test if **at least one** predictor has a significant linear relationship with the response? - **Q:** Why is it "bad" to conduct $p$ hypothesis tests (e.g., at 0.05 level)? ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - If $\beta_1 = \dots = \beta_p=0$, then *for each hypothesis test* with $\alpha=0.05$, there's a 0.05 chance of *falsely* rejecting $H_0: \beta_k = 0$ (Type I error) ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Thus, if $\beta_1 = \dots = \beta_p=0$, then the probability of *falsely* determining that *at least one* predictor is statistically significant: $$ P(\text{reject at least one false rejection of $H_0$}) = 1 - 0.95^p $$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - e.g., with $p=5$, this is 0.2262 - e.g., with $p=14$, this is 0.512 ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Takeaway: We'll often make some mistakes! ::: ## F-Test It would be better to do a hypothesis test for *all* $\beta_k$ *at the same time*: $$ H_0: \beta_1 = \dots = \beta_p = 0 \quad \quad H_A: \text{at least one } \beta_k\neq 0 $$ ::: {.nonincremental} - Called an **F-Test**. - Null sampling distribution follows an "F-Distribution" - Avoids "multiple testing" problem! ::: ## F-Test in `R` ::: {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(mod) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = Balance ~ Limit + Income, data = Credit) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -232.79 -115.45 -48.20 53.36 549.77 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) -385.17926 19.46480 -19.79 <2e-16 *** Limit 0.26432 0.00588 44.95 <2e-16 *** Income -7.66332 0.38507 -19.90 <2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 165.5 on 397 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.8711, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8705 F-statistic: 1342 on 2 and 397 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ::: - Estimated p-value $\approx 0 \implies$ strong evidence to reject $H_0$ - Credit Limit or Income (or both) are associated with Debt Balance # Recap ## Recap ::: {.nonincremental} Today, we reviewed - the linear model and its **assumptions** - **coefficient interpretation** in linear regression - statistical inference: **confidence intervals** and **hypothesis tests**, including the **F-test** :::

      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
